chapters.file: ch03 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy.md
ch04 - Praise.md
ch05 - Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch.md
ch06 - Through a Screen Darkly.md
ch07 - Chapter 01 - Hollywood Doesn’t Know Dick.md
chapters.relation: Ethan Mills opens his 'investigation' of Hollywood's Dick adaptations (Blade Runner, Total Recall, Minority Report, The Adjustment Bureau) by insisting that fan complaints signal something essential lost in translation from print to film, not mere infidelity. He frames the issue as a clash between two philosophical worldviews about free will and knowledge, adopting a bounty-hunter persona to hunt down what Hollywood changed.

chapters.file: ch08 - We Can Conceive It for Ourselves Wholesale.md
chapters.relation: Mills defines the 'Holly-worldview' (good defeats evil, free will secures the triumph of the human spirit, heroes discover truth before the credits roll) and opposes it to the Dickian worldview of paranoia, ignorance and accepted unfreedom, where a 'happy ending' means accepting some inevitable, possibly depressing fact about our place in the universe. He announces the chapter's plan: to test whether the Holly-worldview survives Dick's challenges to its two tenets, free will and knowledge.

chapters.file: ch09 - Free Will at the Box Office.md
chapters.relation: Mills contrasts Dick's 'The Minority Report', where Anderton knowingly kills Kaplan exactly as the final Precog prediction foretold and accepts exile contentedly, with Spielberg's film in which Agatha insists 'You still have a choice' and Crow is spared. He pairs 'Adjustment Team', where Ed Fletcher grovels and accepts the adjustments as for the greater good, with The Adjustment Bureau, where Damon's love teaches the Chairman a lesson and wins the couple their freedom. In both cases the story doubts free will while the movie insists the hero's choice secures human dignity, which Mills attributes to the Dickian worldview being box-office poison rather than to mere economics.

chapters.file: ch10 - Determinism’s Bounty on Free Will.md
chapters.relation: Mills separates determinism from fate: the film's Chairman and his angels override a free humanity, while 'Adjustment Team' depicts an if-then causal order with nothing supernatural being circumvented. He lays out hard determinism (choices caused by brain states and bad noodles leave you 'no better off than an android with false memories') against soft determinism, enlisting Hume's point that without predictable behavior laws like stop signs would be ridiculous. A free action, he argues, needs no uncaused cause: it is unconstrained and flows from your character, as with Anderton's choice to run.

chapters.file: ch11 - Skepticism for Fun and Profit.md
chapters.relation: Mills uses the Blade Runner cuts to stage skepticism: the theatrical happy ending hides the question, the Director's Cut unicorn hints Scott wants Deckard to be a replicant, but Dick's novel has Luba Luft tell Deckard 'You must be an android' and presses him on whether his Voigt-Kampff memories are false, leaving the question unresolved for the reader and for Deckard himself. Since any evidence (empathy, the test's own accuracy) can itself be doubted, the novel is more radically skeptical than the films, because it makes both hypotheses compatible with all the evidence. He then shows Ubik pushing this to the limit, where characters cannot tell what year it is, whether their money is real, or even whether they are alive or dead.

chapters.file: ch12 - What’s So Bad about Determinism.md
ch13 - What’s So Bad about Skepticism.md
chapters.relation: Mills argues that for the ancient skeptics skepticism was the cure, not the disease: Sextus Empiricus prescribes setting equally strong arguments against each other until judgment is suspended and tranquility follows. He reads Nagarjuna and Jayarashi as more radical, using contradictions to uproot the very impulse to hold philosophical views at all, weaning themselves from attachment even to Buddhist views. Applied to Dick, both approaches would have us stop agonizing over whether Deckard is an android or the Ubik characters are dead: the best way to stop worrying is to stop wanting the answers.

chapters.file: ch14 - A Happy Ending.md
ch15 - Chapter 02 - A Quintessence of Dust.md
chapters.relation: Barham breaks down 'what is a replicant' into Aristotle's four causes: efficiently engineered by Tyrell technicians, materially biomechanical, formally modeled on humans, and finally intended for slave labor. Humans can answer the first three causes too, but our final cause, our point or purpose, has no ready answer, and that missing fourth cause is the central theme shared by Blade Runner and Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? as Deckard grapples with his conscience over 'retiring' replicants.

chapters.file: ch16 - Show Me What You’re Made Of.md
chapters.relation: The chapter runs Blade Runner's replicants through Aristotle's list-style test of essences and rejects each candidate: rationality falls when Roy checkmates his own designer at chess and mocks Deckard's panic, agency falls because the replicants set their own agenda by rebelling, and morality falls by reductio, since if morality defined humanity then Deckard's 'retirements' would unmake his, as Roy's jeer 'Aren't you the good man?' underscores. Even love is withheld as sufficient, from Gaff's 'It's too bad she won't live, but then again, who does?' to the distracting detail of Pris's tongue retracting after Roy kisses her corpse.

chapters.file: ch17 - Have You Ever Retired a Human by Mistake.md
chapters.relation: The chapter argues that once Blade Runner has eliminated each candidate essence, 'human' must be treated as an irreducible concept, drawing on Raimond Gaita's example of the racist woman M, who grants Vietnamese people every capacity on the philosopher's list yet remains a racist, and on Simone Weil's claim that every human being is owed obligation simply as a human being. It applies this to Do Androids Dream: Isidore's boss sees past 'chickenhead' prejudice, and Deckard cuts his secretary off before she can label the retired replicants, admitting 'So much for the distinction between authentic living humans and android constructs.' The chapter closes by handing the irreducible concept over to phenomenology and existentialism as methods better suited than necessary-and-sufficient conditions.

chapters.file: ch18 - The Lung-less, All-Penetrating Masterful World-Silence.md
chapters.relation: The section reads Do Androids Dream through Heidegger's 'The Question Concerning Technology': mood organs, empathy boxes, Buster Friendly and catalog-bought animals alienate humans from the world, each other and themselves until only the 'silence of the world' remains, which Isidore theorizes as the inevitable kipple-ization of the universe. Byron's 'Darkness' and Nietzsche's parable of the clever beasts frame Deckard's drive into the dead desert after his last retirement, where he confronts a universe of dead stones that perceive and remember nothing.

chapters.file: ch19 - Do You Think Androids Have Souls.md
chapters.relation: The chapter sets up strong versus weak AI through Rachael's account of the Rosen Association's strategy of iterating models until one is indistinguishable, then brings in Gaita's 'non-speculative conception' of a soul via Wittgenstein's remark that 'My attitude towards him is an attitude towards a soul.' Heidegger's warning that technology tempts us to treat others as mere means is dramatized in Deckard's realization after meeting the predatory bounty hunter Phil Resch that he had been viewing androids, and hence himself, as means; his half-measure of wishing other androids did the retiring shows how far he still has to go.

chapters.file: ch20 - The Cardinal Mystery of Creation.md
chapters.relation: The chapter completes the Heidegger arc: where danger is grows the saving power, so Deckard's first thoughts on finding the toad (U.N. stars and reward money) expose his alienation from any authentic relation to the world, yet he ends 'devoted' to the electric toad because 'The electric things have their lives, too.' Roy Batty's tears-in-rain speech becomes the film's expression of the same saving power: wonder at the mystery of Being is what essentially ensouls humans and replicants alike.

chapters.file: ch21 - Chapter 03 - Dick Doesn’t Do Heroes.md
chapters.relation: Weiss and Nicholas center the chapter on Dick's 1977 Metz interview, where he contrasted Flash Gordon and Buck Rogers heroes who 'give all the answers' with his own 'bumbling, coarse, garrulous' protagonists overwhelmed by an inscrutable universe, echoing Faulkner's Nobel speech about man prevailing through compassion, sacrifice and endurance. They argue Hollywood must inflate these ordinary characters into action figures, and that this very distortion clarifies what Dick was doing: spotlighting human weakness and the occasional rise of average Joes above their 'greedy, incompetent, petty selves.'

chapters.file: ch22 - You’ve Been Adjusted.md
chapters.relation: The chapter tracks the Hollywood upgrades: the 'bald and fat and old' administrator of 'The Minority Report' becomes Tom Cruise, the 'miserable little salaried employee' of 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale' becomes Arnold Schwarzenegger, and real-estate clerk Ed becomes Matt Damon running for Congress. It contrasts The Adjustment Bureau's David Norris, whose defiance of the Chairman's Plan is rewarded with the girl, with Ed Fletcher of 'Adjustment Team', who grovels ('don't de-energize me') and is released only because he is too minor to matter. The upshot: Dick wrote about authenticity, not heroes, and the films swap ordinary endurance for larger-than-life agency.

chapters.file: ch23 - We Can Endorse That for You Wholesale.md
chapters.relation: The chapter opposes Total Recall, where Quaid switches on the alien reactor in 'unwavering faith' and benevolent technology terraforms Mars into a paradise, to 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale', where Quail surrenders because a brain-implanted security device transmits his every thought and 'anything you think may be held against you.' Citing Dick's line that even the most base human schemes are preferable to the most exalted machine tropisms, it argues the films inscribe a faith in technology that Dick himself never held.

chapters.file: ch24 - Nagging Spouses and Robotic Home-Wreckers.md
chapters.relation: The chapter shows Hollywoodization reaching romance: the film gives us a bachelor Deckard and a shy, rescue-worthy Rachael in a classic love story that ends with the couple fleeing together, while the novel gives Deckard a badgering wife Iran and a Rachael Rosen who is a sociopath seducing him precisely so that killing androids like her becomes impossible. Knight-rescues-damsel becomes nebbish-manipulated-by-a-psychopathic-machine, and the chapter insists this wholesale rewriting of Dick's ideas about love and marriage carries philosophical implications that are easy to miss.

chapters.file: ch25 - Scott versus Linklater.md
chapters.relation: The chapter contrasts the directors, Scott's muscular, sensory-assaulting urban noir versus Linklater's quiet, rotoscoped suburban everyday, and their fidelity to the source: quoting Edelstein, Blade Runner misses the novel's empathy-centered psychological complexity, while A Scanner Darkly foregrounds its author with Dick's face appearing in the scramble suit, the closing Author's Note, and Dick's daughters on a faithfully recreated Orange County set. The evaluative criterion throughout is authenticity to Dick, which Linklater preserves and Scott wildly transforms.

chapters.file: ch26 - Deckard versus Arctor.md
chapters.relation: The chapter sets Ford's redemptive Deckard against Keanu Reeves's Bob Arctor, the everyman who spies on himself and disintegrates on Substance D, noting the shared scaffolding (lawman, shadowy supplier Tyrell/New Path, nemesis with doubtful humanity, woman in identity crisis) that only highlights the divergence: Deckard is educated into humanity through Rachael while Arctor is progressively dehumanized, with Donna/Audrey betraying rather than redeeming him. It leans on Dick's 'The Android and the Human' definition of becoming an android as being 'pounded down, manipulated, made into a means without one's knowledge or consent', so that Blade Runner imagines androids becoming human where A Scanner Darkly shows humans becoming androids, with even nature (New Path's corn fields) enlisted in the enslavement.

chapters.file: ch27 - From Hover Cars to Substance D.md
chapters.relation: The chapter contrasts the films' technologies: Blade Runner foregrounds gaudy techno-tropes and a Voight-Kampff machine that discloses the truth about replicants, while A Scanner Darkly dwells on mundane devices, Substance D, surveillance cameras, cell phones and Barris's broken contraptions, that obscure reality and help dissolve Arctor's personality. It reads the latter as Dick's fear of the mechanization of humanity made contemporary, mirroring our own self-documentation on YouTube, Twitter and Facebook, and ending with Bruce, 'a dried husk', in the decoy corn field.

chapters.file: ch28 - Through a Screen, Darkly.md
chapters.relation: The chapter argues A Scanner Darkly is consciously about the media itself: rotoscoping inserts a critical break between viewer and screen, exposing our love of scanning and being scanned, an edge that Hollywood, itself invested in media technology, habitually blunts. Against the blockbuster escape it cites Dick's 'How to Build a Universe that Doesn't Fall Apart Two Days Later', where ordinary people's heroism lies in quiet refusals ('they cannot be compelled to be what they are not'), and ends with Deckard's 'unnatural self' and Arctor's 'soul sickness', both of whom endure, which is where their and our heroism lies.

chapters.file: ch29 - Chapter 04 - Ewe, Robot.md
chapters.relation: Seegert opens with the V-K tortoise scene: Leon knows what a turtle is but cannot feel what it would be like to be one, making empathy the litmus of humanity, even though empathy just is imaginative simulation, so the test ironically demands that humans simulate better than the simulations do. He notes the double irony that replicants show empathy for each other (Roy mourning Pris) while Deckard shoots Zhora in the back without wincing, and that the test's real function is keeping androids enslaveable in an arms race of verisimilitude; the deeper anxiety the chapter sets up is not whether androids can pass for human but whether I might not be human myself.

chapters.file: ch30 - How Animals Make Us Human.md
chapters.relation: The chapter contrasts the novel, where humanity is secured through empathetic relations with scarce real animals (Deckard hating his electric sheep's 'tyranny' because it does not know he exists), with the film, where photographs do the validating: Rachael's 'Look, it's me with my mother' treats the photo as a self-grounding artifact, which the chapter explains via Baudrillard's precession of simulacra, supplemented by Sontag's point that photos act as surrogate relations documenting the loved one's absence. Deckard's piano covered in old sepia photos then reads as overcompensation: abundant evidence, no current relationships, a hint that he may be an android.

chapters.file: ch31 - Narcissism in a “More Human than Human” World.md
chapters.relation: The chapter reads Deckard's longing for a real sheep as a need for his own existence to register on another genuine subjectivity, the electric sheep having no 'there there', as fellow bounty hunter Phil Resch's devotion to his squirrel Buffy implicitly concedes. It then deploys McLuhan's 'Narcissus as Narcosis': technologies like androids, the Penfield Mood Organ and the Empathy Box are a hall of mirrors reflecting humanity back at itself, so Mercerism offers virtual others that 'generate the effects of relationship even if they lack its substance.'

chapters.file: ch32 - Empathy in a “More Human than Human” World.md
chapters.relation: The chapter shows Deckard funding empathy for animals by killing androids, then raises the stakes: since android models keep improving, even close inspection of one's ostensibly 'real' sheep might fail to disclose a clever simulation, which it names as Dick's reconfiguration of the problem of other minds and solipsism. The desert toad, seen 'through Mercer's eyes' and boxed with painstaking care, is revealed by Iran to be electric, so that 'the desert of the real offers safe habitat only for virtual creatures.'

chapters.file: ch33 - The Shock of Being Alive.md
chapters.relation: The chapter fuses McLuhan's narcosis with Heidegger's enframing: technology constrains Being to a human-centered 'world picture' in which forests become board feet and animals become production units, and like Narcissus we fall in love with an image we stamped there ourselves. It enlists the deep ecologists and David Abram ('We are human only in contact, in conviviality, with what is not human') to argue that Dick makes human identity essentially relational, and closes on Baudrillard: digital tweets have become more present for many people than birdsong.

chapters.file: ch34 - The Lives of Electric Others.md
chapters.relation: The chapter follows Deckard past despair at universal fakery (the toad electric, Mercer a set) to his muted epiphany, 'The electric things have their lives, too', and his 'Mercer isn't fake... unless reality is fake', asking whether this extends his circle of moral concern to electric beings or merely concedes the inescapability of virtuality. It reads the film's origami unicorn and Deckard's willingness to make a life with Rachael as parallel acceptances, ending with Iran ordering 'one pound of artificial flies that really fly around and buzz' for the toad her husband is devoted to.

chapters.file: ch35 - Identity Crises.md
ch36 - Chapter 05 - Just Who and How Many Do You Think You Are.md
chapters.relation: Feist opens with Dr. Wigan's autopsy of a man with half a brain and a full mind, moves through the split-brain experiments (the left hand writing 'PIPE' for a concealed pipe as the hemispheres autocomplete each other), and lands on Joseph Bogen's revived thesis that each of us has two minds that merely feel like one. He shows Dick threading Bogen's actual sentences mid-dialogue into A Scanner Darkly so the reader experiences a voice from nowhere, foreshadowing how Arctor's self explodes under the scramble suit, the Fred persona and Substance D into separate persons, Bob and Fred, who end up unsure who, and how many, they are.

chapters.file: ch37 - The User Illusion.md
chapters.relation: The chapter interleaves a doctor's line-card quiz of Fred with Bogen and Wigan's claims that each cerebrum is 'a distinct and perfect whole as an organ of thought' and that our cherished 'inner conviction of Oneness' is mere opinion. Descartes supplies the target: a partless mind known directly and with certainty, external things known only indirectly through possibly misleading ideas, and Dick, we are told, flips this picture so the inside is messy and the outside clear.

chapters.file: ch38 - In a Mirror, Darkly.md
chapters.relation: The chapter stages Arctor's bishop's-robe musing ('What is identity? Where does the act end?') against the classic puzzles: the Ship of Theseus with its two reassembled vessels, and the baby photos you share no cells with. Locke gives memory plus a unified 'thinking, intelligent being' with real unity; Hume bites the bullet, finding only perceptions in introspection, never a self, so the self's identity over time is a normal, inescapable delusion like a mountain's. All of it converges on Fred watching Bob and asking 'who am I? Which one of them is me?'

chapters.file: ch39 - You Don’t Always Get Along.md
chapters.relation: The chapter animates Hume's bundle as a 'little republic' of mental citizens without a universal citizen, staging a dialogue between Person-Hume, who cannot believe there is no self, and Philosopher-Hume, who counsels beer and billiards. It traces the view back to Plato's Republic: the tripartite soul (with Freud's id-ego-superego as a modern rerun), the example of desiring and refusing the same cold beer when you must collect your mother from the airport, and Leontius raging at his own eyes before the corpses, cross-chatter as civil strife among inner citizens, exactly what the doctors diagnose as Fred's symptom.

chapters.file: ch40 - The Outer Workings of the Mind.md
chapters.relation: The chapter has Kant complete the flip of Descartes: we know the self only indirectly and external objects directly, because the mind is a car factory that shapes raw material into everyday experience, so you inspect only the finished products, reverse-engineer the assembly line from them, and the thing in itself stays forever outside knowledge. Rotoscoping becomes the visual correlate: reality is partly constructed by the mind but not totally, and the philosophical task is figuring out which parts of the scene are ours.

chapters.file: ch41 - The Scanner-Self.md
chapters.relation: The chapter identifies Kant's deeper, non-experiencing self, the pure organizer of data behind ordinary experience, as 'a Kantian scanner', then maps the police scanners planted in Arctor's house onto Sartre's analysis of the gaze: another's look downgrades you from observing-subject to observed object, and God's all-penetrating stare would strip you of subjectivity and freedom entirely. Arctor's relentless surveillance culminates in Bruce, the identity-less pure watcher, the scanner-self incarnate, with a closing joke that Facebook profiles are how 'we see ourselves through a profile darkly.'

chapters.file: ch42 - The Valuable Self.md
chapters.relation: The chapter turns from metaphysics to morals: for Kant the self is the most valuable thing in the world, a subject that must never be used as a mere means, since turning a subject into an object is the ultimate immorality. The authorities' plan to hollow Arctor into an unwitting infiltrator, and Donna's lament that he 'didn't volunteer', make the point concrete: what is valuable in us is the self's fuzziness, including its mystery of free will, and to remake a person into a scanner, 'a mere thing that just watches and never chooses', is the ultimate crime.

chapters.file: ch43 - Chapter 06 - Will You Survive a Trip to Rekall, Inc.md
ch44 - Follow the Psyche.md
chapters.relation: The chapter assembles Dick's survival-of-the-psyche cases: Agneta Rautavaara kept alive as a brain in a nutrient bath, Professor Thomas's conscious brain piloting a spaceship, the wub transferring into Captain Franco mid-execution, and the Rexorian consciousness in 'Human Is', then grounds the pattern in Locke's prince-and-cobbler and detached-little-finger thought experiments: 'consciousness makes personal identity.' Everything is codified as the Psyche Continuity Rule, to keep track of the person follow the psyche, with brains mattering only as convenient storage vessels.

chapters.file: ch45 - The Perils of Rekall, Inc.md
chapters.relation: The chapter runs through three incompatible backstories for Total Recall's Quaid, Cohaagen's infiltration plot, Hauser's genuine defection and self-erasure, or a Rekall trip gone live, and shows that in all three no single psyche links the life stages, forcing a Body Continuity Rule and then a Combined Rule that follows the psyche when mental life is unified and the body when it is disjointed. Paycheck's Jennings, who starts referring to his earlier self in the third person, exposes the rule's weak joint: deciding when a mental life counts as sufficiently disjointed.

chapters.file: ch46 - Gotta Have Soul.md
chapters.relation: The chapter tests a Soul Continuity Rule: the wub and Hauser survive because their souls do, though Locke himself denies the soul is the person, and Leibniz's King-of-China bargain, become the richest man if you forget everything, shows why, since it would amount to being annihilated while a King of China is created in your place. Kant's case of one mental life relayed across a chain of souls yields just one person, and the rule's practical failure is evidential: nothing could tell one soul with swapped psyches from swapped souls in the same body.

chapters.file: ch47 - Future Selves and Imposters.md
chapters.relation: The chapter builds a counterexample from Imposter: suppose the same mind-transfer process makes the alien android an imposter in one story but the dying Olham's chosen future self in another, with identical bodily and mental continuity but opposite verdicts, so the Combined Rule fails. Intention cannot rescue the Soul Rule either, since in a government-forced transfer Olham would absurdly have to say 'I am dead over there across the room' if souls simply went where we wanted.

chapters.file: ch48 - Selfless.md
chapters.relation: The chapter concedes that no rule, psyche, body, soul, or combined, accommodates all of Dick's transformations, and refuses to blame Dick for incoherence: his stories force our own conflicting intuitions about wubs, Quaids and downloaded minds into the open. Pessimist, optimist and skeptic each get a verdict, the skeptic's being the chapter's cliffhanger: if we are none of these things, maybe there are no enduring persons at all.

chapters.file: ch49 - Is It Live or Is It Memorex.md
chapters.relation: The chapter supplies the missing detail, transfer versus copying: a 'snapshot' of Olham's brain imprinted on an android leaves Olham where he was, and frying the original destroys him rather than moving him, while the bank-transfer versus copying-money analogy and the question of one psyche imprinted on two androids show why the difference matters. Once the mechanics are filled in one way the alien android is a mere copy and Olham dies, filled in another way he survives bodiless, which restores the Psyche Rule pending a science of how psyches are realized in us.

chapters.file: ch50 - Chapter 07 - Scan Thyself.md
chapters.relation: Butler frames Dick as the latest in philosophy's self-knowledge line: the Delphic 'know thyself' that Socrates made essential to the good life at the cost of his own, the Buddha who sought himself and found only an illusion at the root of suffering, Descartes whose entire philosophy rests on confidence in knowledge of himself as an immaterial being, and Dick's own 8,000-page Exegesis. The chapter's hook is the stakes of self-ignorance (what if you turned out to be something horrible?) and its Dickian version: how do you know you are not an android?

chapters.file: ch51 - How Do You Know You’re Not an Android.md
chapters.relation: The chapter weaponizes the cogito for Deckard's predicament: the fact that 'the lights are on' for you seems to prove you are human, but Descartes' leap from thinking to an immaterial soul is unjustified, since introspection cannot show whether your thoughts run on a soul, a bundle of neurons, or a silicon chip. Hume's 'I never can catch myself at any time without a perception' supplies the precedent, and the conclusion is that no amount of inner experience rules out being an android, so you will have to go take the V-K test after all.

chapters.file: ch52 - The Art of Knowing Arctor.md
chapters.relation: The chapter takes Fred's surveillance of Arctor as a literal solution to the eye-cannot-see-itself problem: split in two, Bob finally observes himself from a detached, evaluative outside, hoping the scanner sees 'clearly' where he sees 'only murk'. Real self-scanning follows, since an fMRI revealing synthetic parts behind your eye sockets would settle the android question and neural correlates might someday sort enduring love from lust, before Alva Noe's Out of Our Heads objection that mental states must be sought in whole organisms interacting with their environments, which would give Arctor's whole-habitat self-scanning the edge over the constrained brain scan.

chapters.file: ch53 - What Does A Scanner See.md
chapters.relation: The chapter answers Arctor's question with Sartre: the gambler cannot observe his way out of deciding again, because consciousness is a nothingness with no determinate essence to be observed, so a scanner used to find yourself 'sees nothing', and Fred watching his own footage is bad faith, hiding from freedom behind presumed facts about himself. Butler then flips the bleakness into Sartre's optimism, reading Dick's 'I myself, I am not a character in this novel: I am the novel' as the author freely remaking his life through the book, his first written without amphetamines, after the break-in he suspected he had staged himself.

chapters.file: ch54 - Phil Chews the Fat.md
chapters.relation: The chapter closes on VALIS's opening gambit, 'I am Horselover Fat, and I am writing this in the third person to gain much-needed objectivity', and Dick's proliferating self-theories (vitamin C overdose, alien telepathy, past lives, Gnostic revelation) across VALIS, Radio Free Albemuth and the Exegesis. Butler weighs the bad-faith reading, that Dick was nailing down a determinate identity to escape the responsibility to choose, against Dick's own android-human essays, in which the authentic human acts spontaneously and throws off masks, concluding that Dick's refusal to settle on any one theory of himself was his playful, Sartrean way of knowing he is not an android.

holes.name: Raimond Gaita
holes.what: Australian philosopher who argues that 'human' is an irreducible moral concept and that in relating to others we have an attitude towards a soul, not an opinion that they have one.
holes.why: Chapter 17 builds its account of what makes us human on Gaita's irreducibility claim and his racist woman 'M' example, and chapter 19 reuses his 'non-speculative conception' of a soul.

holes.name: Simone Weil
holes.what: French philosopher and mystic who held that there is an obligation toward every human being solely in virtue of their humanity, without any further condition.
holes.why: Chapter 17 quotes Weil's (written in occupied France) obligation-to-humanity thesis as the moral anchor for treating 'human' as irreducible.

holes.name: The Irreducibility of the Human
holes.what: The view that no list of capacities (rationality, agency, morality, love) captures what makes someone human; 'human' is a morally irreducible concept grounded in unconditional regard.
holes.why: It is chapter 17's central claim, applied to Isidore the chickenhead and to Deckard's refusal to label the retired androids, after chapter 16 has knocked down each candidate essence.

holes.name: Marshall McLuhan
holes.what: Media theorist who treated technologies as 'extensions of man' that captivate and numb their users, his diagnosis summed up as 'Narcissus as Narcosis'.
holes.why: Chapters 31-33 build their critique of the mood organ, empathy box and electric sheep directly on McLuhan's media-narcosis thesis.

holes.name: Narcissus as Narcosis (technological self-enclosure)
holes.what: McLuhan's claim that technological extensions present our own reflection as an apparent other, numbing us to genuinely different beings.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses it to explain how androids, synthetic sheep and Mercer's empathy box mirror humanity back at itself while posing as others.

holes.name: The Problem of Other Minds
holes.what: The problem that we have access only to others' behavior, never their subjective states, so we can never be certain that apparent others (human, android, or electric animal) have minds at all.
holes.why: Chapter 32 explicitly says Dick reconfigures this classic conundrum, extending the solipsistic worry so that even a 'real' sheep or desert toad may be a simulation.

holes.name: Split-Brain: Two Minds in One Person
holes.what: The thesis, originating with A.L. Wigan and revived by neuroscientist Joseph Bogen, that each cerebral hemisphere supports a distinct mind, so one skull can house two selves.
holes.why: Chapter 36 grounds A Scanner Darkly's Fred/Bob split in Bogen's dual-brain research, quotations from which Dick embeds mid-dialogue in the novel.
